summary:
Project demonstration that gives justice: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvms0xleMYQ

Rimlight is a planner for landing sites and dates at the lunar south pole. It works like booking a flight. You pick a site and a landing date, and Rimlight tells you whether the lander will keep sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio contact for the whole surface stay. If the date is a no-go, a ±5-day scan finds the nearest date that works. An itinerary then proves the verdict: a stay timeline, a 360° horizon profile and a sky chart showing where the terrain blocks the Sun and Earth.

Every number comes from real NASA data. We ray-cast 720-direction horizon masks from LOLA elevation maps and joined them with JPL SPICE ephemerides. Our results match JPL Horizons to under 1 arcsecond and NASA PGDA's 18.6-year illumination maps to within a few percent. A cockpit simulator then flies the booked landing and
replays the real IM-2 "Athena" landing (March 2025), planned versus actual.
This matters because at the south pole a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a lander lives or dies
details:
Project demonstration that gives justice: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvms0xleMYQ

What it does

Rimlight answers a mission planner's question: "If we land here, on this date, do we keep Sun and Earth for the whole stay?" It has three parts

1. Mission Booking. You search a landing the way you'd search a flight. Pick a site (e.g. Mons Mouton, the Shackleton rim, the illumination peaks) and a date, and you get a GO / NO-GO verdict with sunlit %, Earth-visible %, the longest darkness and the longest comms gap. If a date is NO-GO, the ±5-day scan shows the nearest dates that pass. The itinerary backs up each verdict with a stay timeline, a sky chart, a 360° horizon profile, and terrain maps showing which ridge blocks the Sun or Earth, how far away it is and how tall.
2. Cockpit simulator. You "board" your booking and fly from launch to touchdown, with instruments synced to each phase. A voice assistant answers questions like "when do we lose Earth?" or "what if we land two days later?"
3. IM-2 post-mortem. We replay Intuitive Machines' Athena landing, planned site versus actual site and planned time versus actual time. At 80 m resolution, the 369 m miss changed nothing inside the planned 10 days but moved the next sunset 3 h earlier. The ~20 m crater Athena landed in is far smaller than one DEM pixel. That shows both what the data can tell you and where it stops.

How it works

- Ephemeris: Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation from any lunar site, via NASA NAIF SPICE (DE440, MOON_ME frame, light-time and aberration corrections).

- Horizon masks: we cast rays in 720 directions (every 0.5°) across the LOLA 80 m south-pole DEM, with a 240 m far-field layer out to a horizon bound we can

prove. Every committed mask has 0 truncated azimuths.

- Visibility join: the Sun counts as visible when any part of its disc clears the terrain. Hourly samples, with each rise and set refined to under 1 minute.

Results for 2027–2028 are precomputed, so the browser only slices files and never recomputes.

Validation:

- Apollo 11 and 17 Sun/Earth angles match the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.

- Six sites match JPL Horizons to under 1 arcsecond.

- Sunlit and Earth-visible fractions match NASA PGDA's independent 18.6-year visibility maps.

- We injected 11+ deliberate bugs (wrong frame, mirrored azimuth, missing data read as 0, km/m mix-up…) and the test suite catches each one.

Benefits and impact

- Lets planners compare candidate sites and dates in minutes instead of running custom analyses.

- Makes the hard south-pole tradeoff (power vs. comms vs. terrain) visible to non-specialists.

- Learns from a real mission (IM-2) to show which risks the data can and cannot see.

Tools and languages

- Python: SpiceyPy, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, pytest, uv.

- TypeScript/React + Vite, with Vitest checking that the TypeScript metrics match the Python reference.

- Plain HTML/JS/SVG for the booking and cockpit prototypes.

- Vercel for static hosting plus one serverless text-to-speech proxy.

- AI tools: Claude Code, Google Stitch, Google Veo and Gemini TTS (see the SI section).

What makes it creative

- The flight-booking metaphor (with a "boarding pass") turns a dense orbital-mechanics problem into a flow anyone can follow.

- The cockpit lets you fly your plan.

- The real-mission post-mortem grounds it in what actually happened.

What we considered

- Honesty: every number on screen comes from the pipeline. The AI assistant can rephrase answers but is blocked from changing any number.

- Placeholder limits: the GO/NO-GO limits are placeholders, and the app says so.

- Unknown terrain: sites outside the DEM are marked "terrain unknown", never "flat".

- Resolution: we document where 80 m resolution stops being reliable.

- Not certified: the tool supports planning and does not certify a landing.
